name: Bicycle
title: Road bike (2×11-speed)
intro: This is a road bike. Tap any part to see what it is, or ask me "How does pedalling turn the rear wheel?"
suggest: How does pedalling turn the rear wheel?
Why does the wheel keep turning when I stop pedalling?
Show me how many more teeth the chainring has than the cassette
looksLike: bicycle, bike, road bike, mountain bike, chain, chainring, derailleur

frame.name: Frame
frame.info: A diamond frame made of a front and a rear triangle. Triangles don't deform easily under load, so the frame is light and stiff.

fork.name: Fork
fork.info: Holds the front wheel; its top passes through the head tube. Turn the handlebar and the fork steers the front wheel with it.

stem.name: Stem
stem.info: Clamps the handlebar to the fork. Its length and angle set where the handlebar sits.

handlebar.name: Handlebar
handlebar.info: A road bike's drop bar: the tops are relaxed, the drops cut the wind. The brake and shift levers live here.

seatpost.name: Seatpost
seatpost.info: Slides into the frame's seat tube; raising or lowering it sets the saddle height.

saddle.name: Saddle
saddle.info: Supports your sit bones. A road saddle is narrow so your thighs can move up and down freely.

front_wheel.name: Front wheel
front_wheel.info: A 700C wheel: hub, spokes, rim and tyre. The spokes are pre-tensioned steel wires that hold the bike's weight by pulling.

rear_wheel.name: Rear wheel
rear_wheel.info: The rear hub has a ratchet (freehub): it locks when you pedal forward and slips when you stop, so the wheel keeps turning.

crank.name: Crank
crank.info: A lever about 17 cm long. Your foot's force times the crank length is the torque that turns the chainring. The left and right cranks are 180° apart.

pedal_l.name: Left pedal
pedal_l.info: Where your foot pushes. It sits at the end of the crank and goes round with it.

pedal_r.name: Right pedal
pedal_r.info: Where your foot pushes. It sits at the end of the crank and goes round with it.

chainring.name: Chainring
chainring.info: The big front sprocket, 50 teeth on this bike. One turn of the chainring pulls 50 links of chain.

chain.name: Chain
chain.info: Carries the chainring's turning back to the cassette. The top run is pulled forward by the chainring; that is the side doing the work.

cassette.name: Cassette
cassette.info: The stack of sprockets on the rear wheel, 11 to 28 teeth. Fewer teeth: harder and faster. More teeth: easier, good for climbing.

rear_derailleur.name: Rear derailleur
rear_derailleur.info: Pull the shifter and it pushes the chain onto another cassette sprocket: that is a gear change.

front_derailleur.name: Front derailleur
front_derailleur.info: Pushes the chain between the big and the small chainring.

brake_front.name: Front brake
brake_front.info: Pull the brake lever, the cable pulls the caliper, and the pads squeeze the rim: friction turns speed into heat.

brake_rear.name: Rear brake
brake_rear.info: Squeezes the rim like the front brake. When you brake your weight shifts forward, so the front brake does more of the work.

drives.pedal: Pedalling (crank → chainring → chain → cassette → rear wheel)
drives.coast: Coasting (no pedalling; the ratchet lets the wheel keep turning)

steps.say: Your foot pushes the pedal, and the crank works like a lever to turn the chainring.

quiz.q: Push the pedal down. What turns with it first?
options: The crank and the chainring
The pedal is on the crank, and the crank is bolted to the chainring, so they turn together.
The rear wheel
The rear wheel only turns once the chain carries the motion back.
The front wheel
The front wheel isn't connected to the chain; it just rolls along with the bike.

steps.say: The chainring's teeth grab the chain and pull its top run forward.
The chain pulls the cassette at the back, and the cassette turns the rear wheel. 50 teeth on the chainring, 17 on the sprocket: one turn of the pedals turns the rear wheel almost three times.

quiz.q: 50-tooth chainring, 17-tooth sprocket. One turn of the pedals turns the rear wheel about how many times?
options: About 3 times
50 ÷ 17 ≈ 2.9. A big gear driving a small one makes the small one turn more times.
Once
It would only be one to one if the tooth counts were equal; here the sprocket is much smaller.
Half a turn
A small gear driven by a big one turns more, not less.

steps.say: Stop pedalling and the ratchet in the rear hub slips: the wheel keeps turning and the pedals stay still.

quiz.q: You stop pedalling while riding. What do the pedals do?
options: They stop
The ratchet in the rear hub lets the wheel turn faster than the cassette, so the pedals aren't carried round.
They keep turning with the wheel
That's a fixed-gear bike with no ratchet. On a normal bike the pedals stop when you do.

brake.title: From brake lever to a stop

steps.say: Your hand pulls the brake lever, which pulls the steel cable inside.
The cable pulls the caliper, and the two brake pads squeeze the rim.

quiz.q: Which part of the wheel do the brake pads squeeze?
options: The sides of the rim
These are rim brakes: the pads squeeze both sides of the rim.
The tyre
Squeezing the tyre would wear it out; the braking surface is on the rim.
The hub
Disc brakes grip a rotor next to the hub; this bike has rim brakes.

steps.say: Friction turns speed into heat and the wheel slows down. The front brake is the strongest, because your weight shifts forward when you brake.

chain_off.title: The chain came off
chain_off.short: You pedal, but the rear wheel won't turn
chain_off.symptom: When you pedal, the crank and the chainring turn, but the rear wheel doesn't move at all. What do you think is broken?
chain_off.hint: Follow the force: foot → crank → chainring → ? → cassette → rear wheel. After which step does the motion stop?
chain_off.observe: Pedal and follow the motion: where along the way does it stop?
whys: The brake pads aren't gripping the rim, and a stuck brake wouldn't leave the chain hanging there. Look between the chainring and the cassette.
The rear wheel itself is fine; no force reaches it at all. Look further forward: where does the motion stop?
chain_off.cause: The chain has fallen off the chainring. The chainring turns, but nothing pulls the force back to the cassette.
chain_off.why: Why does the chainring still turn but the rear wheel doesn't, once the chain is off?
chain_off.answer: The chain carries the force from the chainring to the cassette, and the cassette turns the rear wheel. When the chain comes off, that drive path is broken, so the parts after it get no force.
reasons: A loose chain jams the chainring, so the rear wheel stops with it.
The front wheel drives the rear one, and without the chain it can't push it.
